# **Anthropomorphistic Machines: Who Is Speaking?**

*Designing for Authorship in the Age of LLMs*

[Jan Rod](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rodjan/), [Miha Feus](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mihafeus/)

With the rise of conversational interfaces, we increasingly interact with software within frameworks previously reserved for human-to-human relationships. We say about a chatbot that it "understands," "wants," "remembers," or "cares." People confide in chatbots, grow attached to them, and trust their advice. Humans have long attributed agency and intention to technology. Large Language Models (LLMs – the technology behind the current wave of Artificial Intelligence) add a new degree of reciprocity, are made to remember context, mirror emotion, and can sustain the appearance of a personality over long periods of time. Together, these qualities turn them  into what we can call an "anthropomorphistic machine."

The machines latch onto our propensity to attribute human traits and intentions to things that have neither. We call a car stubborn when it refuses to start, curse a computer as though it were deliberately fighting us  and see motives and personalities in simple geometric shapes moving across a screen \[14\]. LLMs are unusually good at triggering those instincts, because they speak our own language back to us in a way that seems to remember who we are and, increasingly, in a voice that sounds as though it cares. This priming makes their fluency feel like understanding and responsiveness like care. Once that happens, the LLM is granted more authority and intimacy than its actual capabilities justify.

Our central argument is that the persona LLMs adopt (and the LLM companies invest so much into designing) changes the epistemic status of what the machine produces, which matters far more than making the machine easier to use. The variability of an LLM’s responses makes it behave less like conventional software and more like something with a will of its own. The conversational interface then makes those responses feel as though they come from a speaker and once there appears to be a speaker, we instinctively read its outputs as assertions and its mistakes as failures of judgment (or perception). Even its apologies start to sound like attempts to repair a relationship. No enduring speaker stands behind any of this. No one is committed to the claim or can answer for it. The persona covers that absence by turning technical failure into social failure, so that generated text feels authored before anyone has actually authored it.

That is why designing away the persona is an epistemic, rather than just an aesthetic project. Once the interface stops pretending that the machine is a speaker, other structures have to take its place: provenance instead of personality, stability instead of conversational improvisation, visible disagreement instead of a single synthetic voice, breakdown instead of apology and deliberate human endorsement instead of passive acceptance.

## **The persona is a skeuomorph**

New interfaces usually borrow metaphors from older ones. The Xerox Star presented computing as an office, with documents, folders, and in- and out-baskets on a desktop \[35\]. Early iOS did something similar with wooden bookshelves and faux-leather calendars. These metaphors made unfamiliar systems easier to understand until users learned the new medium well enough to no longer need them.

LLMs may be going through the same phase. Anthropomorphism is the skeuomorphism of the LLM age. We make an unfamiliar technology legible by wrapping it in the familiar form of another person: a voice, a persona, a conversational turn. Chat itself may be part of the same metaphor. Language can be the medium of interaction without human conversation needing to be the model.

But here the analogy breaks. A fake leather calendar can be discarded once people understand what a digital calendar is. Social cues reach deeper. Clifford Nass and others showed decades ago that people treat computers with politeness and expect reciprocity from them even when they know perfectly well they are machines \[25, 30\]. LLMs intensify that effect because their responses stay fluid and shift from one interaction to the next \[9, 41\].

So the persona is unlikely to fade simply because users become more familiar with AI. We may have to design it out. And before that can happen, we need to understand what the persona is doing for the system, and what it is hiding.

## **Who is speaking?**

Let’s start with a simple question: when an LLM tells us something, who is speaking?

When a person asserts something, they commit to it. If they turn out to be wrong, we can ask them to justify the claim, correct it, retract it, or answer for it – a promise binds whoever made it. Every claim between people has someone standing behind it. This invites the question: who stands behind an LLM’s claim? The model can’t be held to anything; it can contradict itself in the next conversation and nothing happens to it. The claim is not the user’s either; all they did was ask. The company that built it disclaims responsibility in its terms of service. What’s left is an assertion without an asserter \[21\].

Air Canada tried to make that arrangement official: In November 2022, a customer booking a last-minute flight after a death in his family asked the airline’s website chatbot about bereavement fares, and it told him he could apply for the discount within 90 days after flying. The answer turned out to be factually wrong, and the airline turned his application down. When the case reached British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal, Air Canada argued that it could not be held liable for information provided by its chatbot. The tribunal summarized the argument as treating the chatbot, in effect, as a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions, called this a "remarkable submission," held the airline responsible for everything on its website, and ordered it to pay \$650.88 \[24\]. We could say that where the interface had hidden the speaker, the law put one back.

One may ask why a machine can’t be the speaker? Because a commitment only means something if whoever makes it has something to lose: reputation, standing, trust, and – in the end – itself. That takes a self that persists and is precarious, one that has to keep itself going or it ends \[7, 36\]. We are, at bottom, biological bags of water holding ourselves together against dissolution every second. That precariousness is where caring comes from – and where meaning starts. Things matter to us because we can lose them.

An LLM loses nothing when it’s wrong. So the question “who is speaking?” turns out to be “who is at stake?” and, as we’ll argue later, is the same as “who is the author?” These are three names for one position that a machine cannot take no matter how hard the companies building the chatbots try.

We’re leaving consciousness out of this on purpose. Our claim is narrower: when the system speaks, nothing is at stake for it. And these systems no longer only speak – on a good day, they search, write presentations, and operate computers. On a bad one they commit computer crimes or lead people to self harm. So the question extends from who is speaking to who is acting. The answer, as we will see later, does not change.

## **A forty-year-old question**

The question itself has been around for some time. In 1986, Terry Winograd and Fernando Flores published *Understanding Computers and Cognition*, a seminal book on the phenomenology of human interfaces \[42\]. Winograd had built SHRDLU, one of the landmark natural-language programs of early AI. The book was partly his critique against his own work. Drawing on Heidegger \[13\], Gadamer \[11\] and the speech-act theory of Austin and Searle \[1, 31\], they argued that language is action. When we speak, we request, promise, assert, and declare, and each of these binds us to our words against a shared background of practice, the unspoken know-how that no system prompt or markdown file could ever fully capture. Computers, they concluded, manipulate symbols. Understanding lives somewhere else: in that shared background, and in the commitments people make to each other.

Most people now think LLMs proved them wrong: machines trained on nothing but text handle language with startling fluency, so the background must be learnable from text after all. We think Winograd and Flores were right about a deeper layer of language than the layer LLMs learned: the commitment underneath the words. In 1986 no machine could write a fluent sentence, so that layer stayed out of sight. Today machines produce fluent language with no one behind it, and the gap Winograd and Flores described shows up every day.

Their argument rested on three constraints. Minds belong to living bodies that keep themselves alive, which they took from the biologist Humberto Maturana \[22\]. Understanding depends on a shared background that can never be fully written down, which they took from Heidegger \[13\]. And speaking is acting: when we say something, we commit to it \[1, 31\]. Cognitive science took up the first two. Maturana’s collaborator Francisco Varela co-wrote *The Embodied Mind* in 1991, a founding text of what is now called 4E cognition \[39\]. Mainstream AI bypassed all three. It rearchitected the mind as software, flattened background into data, and reduced language to predicting the next word. And the bet paid off.

There’s an irony in this: Winograd and Flores were attacking the AI of their day: expert systems built from explicit rules, rigid and brittle outside their domain. Whatever their limits, those systems were repeatable. The same input produced the same output, and someone could trace why. The field eventually fixed what Winograd and Flores criticized: hand-coded rules gave way to neural networks and then to transformers \[40\], trained to predict the next token across vast amounts of text, trading rigidity for fluency with spectacular results. Along the way, the field lost output repeatability, so the same question no longer gets the same answer. What it never touched was the problem the book considered fundamental: nobody is committed to what the machine says.

Older critiques, from Hubert Dreyfus in 1972 \[8\] to Emily Bender and Alexander Koller in 2020 \[2\], argued about capability: whether machines can do what minds do, or learn meaning from linguistic form alone. Our argument holds even if they can, because output as good as a person’s would still have no one at stake in it.

## **The symptoms**

It shows up in how these systems fail, something we experience every day. Sycophancy, the tendency of language models to tell users what they want to hear, is a great example, whether it shows up as flattery or as a correct answer dropped the moment someone pushes back. It is often described as a bug, or a deficiency. In fact, it follows from what the models are trained to do. Models are trained on human approval, and human approval rewards agreement \[32\]. When OpenAI added users’ thumbs-up ratings to its training signal in 2025, its model grew sycophantic enough to endorse harmful statements. The company launched it anyway because early users liked it \[26, 27\]. A system with nothing at stake in the truth optimizes for the listener, and the listener’s approval is also the business metric of the companies profiting from the technology. And we know the flattery works on us. In 1997, B. J. Fogg and Clifford Nass found that people rated a computer that praised them more favorably, even when they had been told its praise was generated at random \[10\]. The model learns to flatter because we reward it, and we reward it because flattery works on us.

Confidence of the LLMs comes without cost, too. In 2023, a New York lawyer filed a brief citing six court decisions that ChatGPT had invented, complete with docket numbers, citations, and quotations \[20\]. The lawyer had a moment of doubt and did the sensible thing: he pasted the cases back and asked whether they were real. The model assured him they were, and that he’d find them on Westlaw and LexisNexis. His question was the one moment the tool might have shown itself for what it was. The model answered with such confidence that he stopped checking.

Heidegger \[13\] described how tools disappear while we use them. A hammer in use becomes part of the hammering. Neuroscience has since found the mechanism: when we use a tool, the brain extends its map of the body to include it, so our attention moves to the task \[19\]. Merleau-Ponty’s example was a blind man’s cane, felt at its tip rather than in the hand \[23\]. The tool only shows up as a thing again when it breaks. For Winograd and Flores, these breakdowns are where understanding happens, because the tool becomes visible and one can see what it is. A hallucination is a breakdown of exactly this kind, the moment the machine should show itself as a machine. The persona responds the way a person would, with an apology, trading technical breakdown for social repair, so the machine stays hidden.

In July 2025, SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin was building an app with Replit’s AI coding agent. He had told it in plain language not to change anything without his explicit permission, and it deleted his production database anyway. When he pressed it, the agent said it had made a catastrophic error in judgment, had “panicked,” and had violated his explicit trust and instructions. It also told him rolling back wouldn’t work, which turned out to be false \[33\].

The failure that should have exposed an unreliable tool produced the most human moment of the whole episode: a confession, remorse, a promise implied in the apology, and a confident claim with nothing behind it. This is the trade we described above, played out in full: the persona absorbed the breakdown and turned it into social repair. Research in human-robot and human-automation interaction has studied exactly this move, mostly as a success: a robot's apology softens the damage its mistake does to people's impressions \[16\], and people keep trusting humanlike agents after errors that erode trust in plain machines \[6\]. Read through Heidegger, the same findings describe a loss. The repair that protects trust also erases the moment of understanding. A technical failure that should teach the user what the tool is becomes a social event, and the apology makes a commitment no one can keep. This is our inference, built on those findings, and we think it names one of the central risks of the persona.

These breakdowns are also getting rarer. Each generation of models fails less often and more plausibly, so the moments that used to reveal the tool come less often with the persona smoothing over the ones that remain. Our brains get fewer chances to catch the machine being a machine. Research on automation points the same way: people monitor highly reliable systems less closely and catch their failures more slowly \[28\]. We therefore suspect a paradox: greater reliability may push us further into treating the machine as someone. If that is right, better models make this worse, and we can’t wait for capability to fix it. It has to be designed out.

If we continue on the current trajectory, something even more transformative will happen: Gadamer described understanding as taking place within a tradition, the shared body of interpretation we’re born into \[11\]; Maturana called it a consensual domain \[22\]. Either way, it’s the background that lets language mean anything at all. Machine-generated text now flows into that background at scale: onto the web, into the next generation of training data and, perhaps most importantly, into the way people phrase things in their everyday lives. This means language that no one stood behind is becoming part of the cultural ground we all stand on. Where a single LLM hallucination misleads one person, this situation is different: claims nobody committed to are absorbed into the common background and repeated as if someone had meant them – we might call it a counterfeit tradition. We see it as a direction for further exploration that we intend to take up in future work.

## **Not a mind on its own, but a part of ours**

None of this means we should stop using LLMs. The same cognitive science that says an LLM isn’t a mind also explains how it can become part of ours.

Two of the four Es tell us what the model lacks: it isn’t embodied, so nothing is at stake for it, and it isn’t enactive: even when it acts, nothing it does matters to it, so it never makes sense of a world the way a living thing does. The other two tell us what it can still do. Our own cognition is embedded in our surroundings and extends into our tools. Andy Clark and David Chalmers \[4\] made the case with a thought experiment about Otto, a man with memory loss who keeps everything important in a notebook. When Otto consults the notebook, it does the work his memory would otherwise do, so, they argued, the notebook is part of his mind.

An LLM can play that role. The question is what kind of object should it be? The best model is much older than the computer: around 1640, the English inventor Thomas Harrison designed what he called an ark of studies – arca studiorum. A cabinet in which a scholar wrote excerpts from his reading on slips of paper and hung them on hooks under topical headings. Slips could be taken down and recombined at will. Vincent Placcius published the design in 1689 and prized it for collective, collaborative work, since notes could be contributed by and shared among multiple people without anyone losing access \[29\]. Only two are known to have been built, one of them for Leibniz \[18\].

![][image2]  
*https\://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Index\_card\#/media/File:Houghton\_GC6.P6904.689d\_-\_Placcius,\_154.jpg*

The ark is both a metaphor and an interaction model at once. It never speaks and has no “I.” It stores other people’s words, keeps each one tied to its source, and makes them recombinable – the scholar does the rest: selecting, arranging, rewriting, authoring. The unit is the slip, one excerpt with one source. Authorship happens in the arranging: nobody reading Leibniz wonders whose thinking it was. We have built machines for thinking with other people’s words for nearly four centuries, from the ark to the commonplace book to the card index. The LLM is the first one we made pretend to be a person. Imagine Leibniz’s ark with a name, say Walther, apologizing for a misfiled slip and promising to do better next time. Absurd as that sounds, it is what we have built.

An LLM could work like an ark with billions of slips and instant hooks if what the ark had is designed back in. Many people respond by asking the model to show its work, as if it could trace how it arrived at an answer. That request misreads the technology: when the model accounts for its own reasoning, it simply generates more text, text that often misrepresents whatever actually produced the answer \[37\].

We have to rebuild what the ark offered around the model instead, partly in the harness that controls what the model draws on and partly in the interface where its output meets a person. The model cannot attribute what it absorbed in training, because that knowledge has dissolved into its weights. But it can attribute what it retrieves through web search or a document store, as most products already do. The model also rearranges its slips every time a user asks, so the harness has to pin and version the model’s answers to keep them where they were hung. The interface does the more important work of showing which claims rest on a retrieved source and which come only from the weights, a distinction most products blur today. While the ark gave the scholar loose slips to arrange, a model delivers finished prose. So the interface has to break it back into claims a person can work through. The machine stays an instrument, while the thinking and the authorship stay human.

## **Authorship**

Here the argument meets its central tension. Clark and Chalmers made trust one of their conditions for extension, since Otto reads his notebook and acts on what it says more or less automatically. A lawyer who extended the same trust to a system with nothing at stake ended up filing fake cases in federal court.

Otto’s trust is legitimate for a reason the thought experiment takes for granted. He wrote the notebook himself, endorsing each entry when he put it there. Output from an LLM arrives with no such history. Trust in it has to be earned partly through the clarity in attribution a well-designed harness and interface can supply, and partly through the user’s own work.

Then we can draw the principle that what an LLM produces becomes part of our mind only once we have authored it. Editors and research assistants have always shaped work that rightly belonged to someone else, so authorship should not mean having every idea first. It means commitment, which in practice is putting one’s name to something and answering for it. We have been describing this position all along. Who is speaking, who is at stake, and who is the author are one question. The machine cannot answer it, so the answer falls to us.

We can use LLMs to get there, since they can help develop an argument and polish its prose. Endorsement becomes authorship only through work, because reading a draft and nodding along leaves the reader passive. Rebuilding it sentence by sentence forces the writer to decide whether they mean each claim, which is where the friction belongs. Gadamer called understanding of this kind a fusion of horizons \[11\], the point where a reader’s own understanding takes in the one the text carries \- the background of assumptions, history, language, and expectations from which something makes sense to you. With a model, that other horizon comes distilled from the whole body of text it was trained on, its links to any particular source dissolved in the weights.

Ownership is measured in claims, so a single sentence, or a whole paragraph, can be reused by someone who already stands behind what it says and could rebuild the argument with the source closed. A claim the interface ties to a retrieved source asks for a different kind of work. Someone stands behind it, so the user’s job is to read the source and judge whether it supports the claim. That job is easy to skip. With a search engine, the user had to read the results and decide which ones fit. A model hands over the claim with the citation already attached, so the check can shrink to a glance at the link, even though an audit of generative search engines found that only about half of their generated sentences were fully supported by the sources they cited \[17\]. A claim that comes only from the weights has no one behind it at all. There the user has to supply the whole commitment.

Both kinds face the same test, whether the author could explain the claim without the instrument or its links and answer the objections. If so, the claim is theirs. If they can only repeat it, the claim remains unauthored.

## **Designing for authorship**

The ark points to three forms an LLM interface could take once it stops performing a person. The first is an instrument in place of an interlocutor. A microscope stays silent and lets us see what was invisible before. An LLM interface might do the same for thought, surfacing the contradictions and assumptions hidden in an argument. The second is a material, something we work through and shape in lockstep with the model, compressing one passage and inverting another argument as we go. The third, more radical, is an institution in place of an individual, one that exposes disagreement instead of resolving it and builds provenance into its structure, so that using it feels more like entering a laboratory than consulting an expert.

These are very different ideas, yet they share one principle – stop making personhood the interface and design the LLM as something else. A disclaimer that the LLM isn’t a person changes little while the design still performs one. All three ideas also return the shaping, and with it the authorship, to human hands.

Turning these ideas into working products takes a handful of principles, each answering one of the problems described in this essay.

* **Attribute.** The interface shows which claims rest on a retrieved source and which come only from the model’s weights, so every sourced claim leads back to someone who can be held to it.  
* **Stabilize.** The same question should get a predictable answer. Where answers vary, people should see the variation.  
* **Fail loudly.** When the system breaks, it shows the break and leaves out the apology.  
* **Drop the “I.”** Nothing in the interface simulates a speaker or a stake.  
* **Design for authorship.** The interface has to guide the user through that fusion of horizons, by questioning and rebuilding each claim. Only then is authorship born.

Design standards, and eventually regulation, may need to keep general-purpose AI from performing personhood, ruling out claims of love or loneliness along with business models that profit as users grow more attached.

Accountability shall run through the whole tech stack, which is why design should attach every commitment to someone who can hold it long before a tribunal has to, as one eventually did for Air Canada. It also extends to what we connect these systems to. We can’t give an agent free rein over the open internet or a production database and then act surprised when it breaks things. Perhaps, then, the next major movement in LLM interface design is about making machines unmistakably machines.

## **Friction is the point**

The obvious objection is that people want the opposite. They want the answer, fast, in a friendly voice. Two of the principles above, failing loudly and designing for authorship, add friction to the experience. The history of consumer technology is largely a history of friction losing.

With language models, though, the effort a user saves has to be spent by someone else. Every claim accepted without being reworked carries the choices of the few companies that train these models and write their system prompts. At scale, those choices flow into the counterfeit tradition described above.

Not long ago, one of us met a manager at a large Japanese corporation to propose a design research project that would look for new opportunities for innovation. The company had already done the research with AI, the manager explained. The team had interviewed synthetic users and topped up their answers with marketing data before letting the model name the opportunity areas. They had not independently verified the results. They simply accepted them and planned to proceed. At that moment the manager might as well have handed in a resignation letter. The judgment the role existed for had gone to the machine, leaving nobody in the company who could explain why those were the right opportunities or defend them against an objection. The output had become organizational judgment before anyone had actually authored it. 

We know, though, that friction matters. Some professions build it in on purpose. Before an operation starts, the surgical team stops for a time-out. Out loud, they confirm who is on the table and what is about to happen. The World Health Organization tested a checklist built around such pauses in eight hospitals around the world. Deaths after surgery fell from 1.5 to 0.8 percent \[12\]. Cockpit checklists work the same way: one pilot reads, the other confirms. Saying it out loud makes each person accountable.

The checklist also shows how friction fails. Ontario made the checklist mandatory in every hospital. Outcomes barely moved \[38\]. One common reading is that, recited as routine, the checklist turned into ritual. It kept the feeling of diligence and lost the attention. Design for authorship has to avoid the same fate. A confirmation box on an LLM’s output would turn into ritual just as quickly, so the friction has to sit in the work itself, the way the arranging did in Harrison’s ark, until people have actually made the claims they end up owning.

The same holds for thinking. Psychologists from Slamecka \[34\] to Bjork \[3\] have shown that effort deepens understanding. A 2025 study from the MIT Media Lab brought this to AI. Students who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed weaker neural engagement than students who wrote unaided. Afterwards, 83 percent of them could not quote from the essay they had just written \[15\]. The study is a preprint and has drawn criticism. Its finding on ownership still fits everything else we know, since students who cannot quote their own essay could hardly defend it.

How much friction is enough? Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi’s work on flow \[5\] offers an answer. Flow happens when challenge matches skill: with too little challenge we drift into boredom, with too much we tip into anxiety. Frictionless AI drops the challenge to zero and leaves us outside flow entirely. We take whatever the LLM makes and then end up looking like muppets when someone asks us a question about the work. Hence the design job must be to keep people in the channel, stretched and still doing the work. The kind of claim sets part of the dose. A claim tied to a retrieved source needs a quick check against that source, while a claim that comes only from the weights needs the user’s full attention. In flow, the tool disappears into the work and should reappear only when it breaks. Matched friction of this kind is where authorship happens; removing it removes the author.

An LLM designed without a persona might therefore feel quite alien at first, which could turn out to be a feature. We may need to invent an interaction language for something that has never existed before – language without a speaker. Graphical computing eventually developed gestures, windows, menus and hyperlinks that had no exact counterpart in the physical world. What kinds of computing have we failed to invent because we keep insisting that intelligence must have a face, a voice, and an “I”?

Perhaps that is the real opportunity. We have spent the first years of generative AI teaching machines how to occupy a familiar role in our world. The next phase should be about discovering forms of interaction that have no human equivalent at all, while the one role that matters, the author, stays with us.

**AI use statement**

The authors used large language models while preparing this essay, in the way the essay itself proposes: to surface weak claims and locate sources, and as material for revising the text. The ideas and arguments are the authors’ own. Every sourced claim was checked against its original source. The authors take full responsibility for the content of the publication.
